claim: In low-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, malaria continues to be a major cause of mortality.
source: In low-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, malaria continues to be a major cause of mortality, and intense efforts are underway to eliminate Plasmodium falciparum parasites, which cause the most severe form of the disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of malaria mortality in low-income countries, particularly sub-Saharan Africa, which is established knowledge in the field of global health.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum parasites cause the most severe form of malaria.
source: In low-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, malaria continues to be a major cause of mortality, and intense efforts are underway to eliminate Plasmodium falciparum parasites, which cause the most severe form of the disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the severity of P. falciparum malaria compared to other Plasmodium species.

claim: The Greater Mekong Subregion has repeatedly been the origin of drug-resistant malaria strains.
source: This problem is most acutely felt in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS), a region that has repeatedly been the origin of drug-resistant strains (Dondorp et al., 2009; Noedl et al., 2008; Plowe, 2009; Roper et al., 2004; Mita et al., 2011) and in neighboring countries including Bangladesh and India, where resistance could be imported.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed publications.

claim: The GMS is a region of relatively low endemicity, with entomological inoculation rates 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than in Africa.
source: The GMS is a region of relatively low endemicity, with entomological inoculation rates 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than in Africa, where the vast majority of cases occur (Chaumeau et al., 2018; Hay et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research comparing entomological inoculation rates between GMS and Africa.

claim: Infections in the GMS are most common amongst individuals who work in or live near forests in remote rural parts of the region.
source: Infections are most common amongst individuals who work in or live near forests in remote rural parts of the region (Cui et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A high proportion of individuals in the GMS are immunologically naïve and develop symptoms that require treatment when infected.
source: Since infections are infrequent, a high proportion of individuals in this region are immunologically naïve, and develop symptoms that require treatment when infected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low endemicity and infrequent infections mentioned earlier in the text.

claim: High parasite exposure to drugs may be a major evolutionary driving force for the emergence of genetic factors that confer resistance to frontline therapies in the GMS.
source: This results in high parasite exposure to drugs, which may be a major evolutionary driving force for the emergence of genetic factors that confer resistance to frontline therapies (Escalante et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Drug resistance alleles emerged in the GMS and subsequently spread to Africa multiple times in the past.
source: In the past, drug resistance alleles emerged in the GMS and subsequently spread to Africa multiple times, rolling back progress against the disease at the cost of many lives (Mita et al., 2009; Trape et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Artemisinin combination therapies (ACTs) are the frontline therapy of choice worldwide for malaria.
source: Currently, global malaria control and elimination strategies depend on the efficacy of artemisinin combination therapies (ACTs) which are the frontline therapy of choice worldwide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current malaria treatment guidelines.

claim: Parasite strains resistant to artemisinin have emerged in the GMS.
source: Hence, in view of the emergence in the GMS of parasite strains resistant to artemisinin (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ashley et al., 2014; MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016) and its ACT partner drug piperaquine, (Amaratunga et al., 2016; van der Pluijm et al., 2019; Leang et al., 2015; Spring et al., 2015) the elimination of P. falciparum from this region has become a global health priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Parasite strains resistant to piperaquine have emerged in the GMS.
source: Hence, in view of the emergence in the GMS of parasite strains resistant to artemisinin (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ashley et al., 2014; MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016) and its ACT partner drug piperaquine, (Amaratunga et al., 2016; van der Pluijm et al., 2019; Leang et al., 2015; Spring et al., 2015) the elimination of P. falciparum from this region has become a global health priority.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The elimination of P. falciparum from the GMS has become a global health priority.
source: Hence, in view of the emergence in the GMS of parasite strains resistant to artemisinin (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ashley et al., 2014; MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016) and its ACT partner drug piperaquine, (Amaratunga et al., 2016; van der Pluijm et al., 2019; Leang et al., 2015; Spring et al., 2015) the elimination of P. falciparum from this region has become a global health priority.
evidence: This is an inference based on the emergence of drug resistance and its implications for global health.

claim: NMCPs make extensive use of clinical and epidemiological data in their assessments.
source: In these assessments, NMCPs make extensive use of clinical and epidemiological data, such as those from routine clinical reporting and therapy efficacy studies.
evidence: This is a statement about current practices of National Malaria Control Programmes.

claim: Parasite genetic data is less frequently available to NMCPs and typically restricted to single genetic variants or small numbers of sites.
source: Parasite genetic data is less frequently available, and typically restricted to single genetic variants (Ménard et al., 2016), or small numbers of sites where quality sample collection protocols could be executed (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Routine mapping of a broad set of resistance markers can keep NMCPs abreast of the spread of resistance strains.
source: However, routine mapping of a broad set resistance markers can keep NMCPs abreast of the spread of resistance strains, and help them predict changes in drug efficacy and assess alternative therapies, especially if dense geographical coverage allows mapping of resistance at province or district level.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential benefits of genetic surveillance.

claim: The increased affordability of high-throughput sequencing technologies offers new opportunities for delivering genetic knowledge to public health.
source: The increased affordability of high-throughput sequencing technologies now offers new opportunities for delivering such knowledge to public health, supporting the optimization of interventions where resources are limited (Nagar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about technological opportunities.

claim: Cost-effective implementation of genomic technologies can make important contributions to malaria elimination.
source: Cost-effective implementation of genomic technologies, aimed at supporting public health decision-making, can make important contributions to malaria elimination (Desmond-Hellmann, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: GenRe-Mekong analyzes small dried blood spots samples that are easy to collect at public health facilities from patients with symptomatic malaria.
source: GenRe-Mekong analyzes small dried blood spots samples, which are easy to collect at public health facilities from patients with symptomatic malaria, and uses high-throughput technologies to extract large amounts of parasite genetic information from each sample.
evidence: This is a description of the GenRe-Mekong methodology.

claim: GenRe-Mekong uses high-throughput technologies to extract large amounts of parasite genetic information from each sample.
source: GenRe-Mekong analyzes small dried blood spots samples, which are easy to collect at public health facilities from patients with symptomatic malaria, and uses high-throughput technologies to extract large amounts of parasite genetic information from each sample.
evidence: This is a description of the GenRe-Mekong methodology.

claim: GenRe-Mekong has worked with NMCPs in Cambodia, Vietnam, Lao PDR (Laos), Thailand, and Bangladesh.
source: To date, GenRe-Mekong has worked with NMCPs in Cambodia, Vietnam, Lao PDR (Laos), Thailand, and Bangladesh and has supported large-scale multisite research and elimination projects across the region (van der Pluijm et al., 2019; von Seidlein et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2019; Landier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the project's collaborations, supported by citations.

claim: GenRe-Mekong has processed 9623 samples from eight countries.
source: The project has processed 9623 samples from eight countries, delivering data to the 12 studies that submitted samples.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the project's output.

claim: GenRe-Mekong has delivered data to 12 studies that submitted samples.
source: The project has processed 9623 samples from eight countries, delivering data to the 12 studies that submitted samples.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the project's output.

claim: GenRe-Mekong analysis pipelines translate genotypes into predictions of drug resistance phenotypes.
source: To facilitate integration into NMCP decision-making workflows, our analysis pipelines translate genotypes into predictions of drug resistance phenotypes, and present these as maps which are easily interpreted by public health officials with no prior training in genetics.
evidence: This is a description of the GenRe-Mekong methodology.

claim: In Laos and Vietnam, GenRe-Mekong is implemented in dozens of public health facilities in endemic provinces.
source: In Laos and Vietnam, where GenRe-Mekong is implemented in dozens of public health facilities in endemic provinces, results from GenRe-Mekong have been used by NMCPs in assessments of frontline therapy options and resource allocation to combat drug resistance.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the project's implementation.

claim: Results from GenRe-Mekong have been used by NMCPs in Laos and Vietnam in assessments of frontline therapy options and resource allocation to combat drug resistance.
source: In Laos and Vietnam, where GenRe-Mekong is implemented in dozens of public health facilities in endemic provinces, results from GenRe-Mekong have been used by NMCPs in assessments of frontline therapy options and resource allocation to combat drug resistance.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the project's impact on public health decision-making.

claim: Aggregated data from multiple studies within GenRe-Mekong have powered large-scale genetic and clinical studies of resistance to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ).
source: Aggregated data from multiple studies within GenRe-Mekong have powered large-scale genetic and clinical studies of resistance to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ), revealing a regional cross-border spread of specific strains (van der Pluijm et al., 2019; Hamilton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GenRe-Mekong data have revealed a regional cross-border spread of specific DHA-PPQ resistant strains.
source: Aggregated data from multiple studies within GenRe-Mekong have powered large-scale genetic and clinical studies of resistance to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ), revealing a regional cross-border spread of specific strains (van der Pluijm et al., 2019; Hamilton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GenRe-Mekong conducts whole-genome sequencing of selected high-quality samples.
source: To power such high-resolution genetic epidemiology analyses of population structure and gene flow, GenRe-Mekong conducts whole-genome sequencing of selected high-quality samples, contributing to the open-access MalariaGEN Parasite Observatory (http://www.malariagen.net/resource/26) (Pearson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the GenRe-Mekong methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: As of August 2019, GenRe-Mekong has partnered with NMCPs in five countries to conduct large-scale genetic surveillance and epidemiological surveys.
source: As of August 2019, GenRe-Mekong has partnered with NMCPs in five countries to conduct large-scale genetic surveillance (Vietnam, Laos), smaller-scale pilot projects (Cambodia, Thailand), and epidemiological surveys (Bangladesh).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the project's collaborations as of a specific date.

claim: A total of 9623 samples from eight countries have been processed by GenRe-Mekong as of August 2019.
source: A total of 9623 samples from eight countries have been processed in this period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the project's output, supported by a figure reference.

claim: The majority of samples (n=6905, 72%) were collected in GMS countries (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar).
source: The majority of samples (n=6905, 72%) were collected in GMS countries (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar), but GenRe-Mekong also supported projects submitting samples from Bangladesh, India, and DR Congo (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sample distribution.

claim: The vast majority of processed samples were collected prospectively (n=9002, 93.5%).
source: The vast majority of processed samples were collected prospectively, under partnership agreements with GenRe-Mekong (n=9002, 93.5%); two research projects submitted retrospective samples collected in the period 2012–2015 (n=621, 6.5%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sample collection timing.

claim: Approximately 59% of samples (n=5716) were submitted by NMCP partnerships.
source: Approximately 59% of samples (n=5716) were submitted by NMCP partnerships, whose contribution increased over time as surveillance projects ramped up (43.4% in 2016, vs. 94.6% in 2018, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sample sources.

claim: NMCP partnership contribution to samples increased from 43.4% in 2016 to 94.6% in 2018.
source: Approximately 59% of samples (n=5716) were submitted by NMCP partnerships, whose contribution increased over time as surveillance projects ramped up (43.4% in 2016, vs. 94.6% in 2018, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about temporal trends in sample sources.

claim: GenRe-Mekong samples consist of dried blood spots (DBSs) on filter paper.
source: GenRe-Mekong samples consist of dried blood spots (DBSs) on filter paper.
evidence: This is a description of the sample type used in the project.

claim: DNA extracted from samples was selectively amplified to increase the proportion of parasite DNA and reduce human DNA contamination before genotyping.
source: DNA extracted from the samples was selectively amplified (Oyola et al., 2016) to increase the proportion of parasite DNA and reduce human DNA contamination before genotyping (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: SpotMalaria genotypes different types of variants including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), copy number variations and sequences of gene domains.
source: The production of genetic report cards involves genotyping different types of variants: single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), copy number variations and sequences of gene domains.
evidence: This is a description of the SpotMalaria platform capabilities.

claim: In the initial phase, SpotMalaria used capillary sequencing of the kelch13 gene to detect SNPs associated with artemisinin resistance.
source: In the initial phase, SpotMalaria used a mixture of technologies: capillary sequencing of the kelch13 gene to detect SNPs associated with artemisinin resistance (Ashley et al., 2014; Ariey et al., 2014); and high-throughput mass spectrometry to genotype SNP variants.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology, supported by citations.

claim: SpotMalaria was later replaced with an amplicon sequencing process based on short-read deep sequencing of specific portions of the parasite genome.
source: This was later replaced with an amplicon sequencing process, based on short-read deep sequencing of specific portions of the parasite genome, supporting a high degree of multiplexing (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the evolution of the methodology.

claim: A total of 3473 samples (36%) were processed by the amplicon sequencing platform.
source: A total of 3473 samples (36%) were processed by the amplicon sequencing platform, which delivered a higher genotyping success rate than the earlier process (94% vs 82% mean success rate for genetic barcode positions).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the methodology and its performance.

claim: The amplicon sequencing platform delivered a higher genotyping success rate than the earlier process (94% vs 82% mean success rate for genetic barcode positions).
source: A total of 3473 samples (36%) were processed by the amplicon sequencing platform, which delivered a higher genotyping success rate than the earlier process (94% vs 82% mean success rate for genetic barcode positions).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of methodology performance.

claim: The vast majority of samples were taken from malaria patients upon admission (92%, n=8866).
source: The vast majority of samples were taken from malaria patients upon admission (92%, n=8866).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sample collection timing.

claim: Genotypes at mitochondrial positions provided confirmation of the infecting parasite species.
source: Genotypes at mitochondrial positions provided confirmation of the infecting parasite species: P. falciparum (Pf), P. vivax (Pv), P. knowlesi (Pk), P. malariae (Pm), and P. ovale (Po).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for species identification.

claim: All five Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. knowlesi, P. malariae, and P. ovale) were detected in the dataset.
source: All five species were detected in our dataset: non-Pf parasites were found in 8.8% of samples (n=745 out of 8486 samples for which species could be determined).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about species detection in the dataset.

claim: Non-P. falciparum parasites were found in 8.8% of samples (n=745 out of 8486 samples for which species could be determined).
source: All five species were detected in our dataset: non-Pf parasites were found in 8.8% of samples (n=745 out of 8486 samples for which species could be determined).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about species distribution in the dataset.

claim: P. vivax was the most commonly detected non-P. falciparum species (317 Pf/Pv mixed infections, and 405 Pv-only infections).
source: Pv was the most commonly detected non-Pf species (317 Pf/Pv mixed infections, and 405 Pv-only infections), followed by Pk (11 Pf/Pk and 6 Pk-only infections), while Pm and Po were detected in three and two samples, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about species distribution in the dataset.

claim: GenRe-Mekong produces a genetic barcode for each sample constructed by concatenating the alleles at 101 SNPs distributed across all nuclear chromosomes.
source: Genetic barcodes are constructed by concatenating the alleles at 101 SNPs distributed across all nuclear chromosomes (see Materials and methods), chosen on the basis of their geographically widespread variability and their power to recapitulate genetic distance.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for genetic barcode construction.

claim: Genetic barcodes can be used to detect loss of diversity due to demographic effects.
source: Genetic barcodes can be used to detect loss of diversity due to demographic effects, (Daniels et al., 2015) or to compare parasites from the same patient to distinguish recrudescences from reinfections (Felger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Genetic barcodes can be used to compare parasites from the same patient to distinguish recrudescences from reinfections.
source: Genetic barcodes can be used to detect loss of diversity due to demographic effects, (Daniels et al., 2015) or to compare parasites from the same patient to distinguish recrudescences from reinfections (Felger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A neighbor-joining tree derived from genetic distance estimates clearly separates parasites from the Thai-Myanmar border region from those circulating along the Thai-Cambodian border.
source: For example, a neighbor-joining tree derived from these genetic distance estimates (Figure 2) clearly separates parasites from the Thai-Myanmar border region from those circulating along the Thai-Cambodian border, consistent with findings from WGS analyses (Miotto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure and a citation to published research.

claim: 827 samples failed to produce barcodes due to low P. falciparum DNA content.
source: We used genetic barcode results to discard 827 samples that failed to produce barcodes due to low Pf DNA content.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sample quality filtering.

claim: The final set of 7626 P. falciparum samples corresponds to 90.2% of all P. falciparum-containing samples taken upon admission.
source: This yielded a final set of 7626 Pf samples, corresponding to 90.2% of all Pf-containing samples taken upon admission, which provided the data used for epidemiological analyses.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the final dataset used for analysis.

claim: GenRe-Mekong produces genotypes covering a broad range of known variants associated to drug resistance.
source: GenRe-Mekong produces genotypes covering a broad range of known variants associated to drug resistance (Table 2) to support assessment of the spread and risk of drug resistance.
evidence: This is a description of the project's capabilities, with reference to a table.

claim: GenRe-Mekong uses genotypes to derive predicted phenotypes based on a set of rules derived from peer-reviewed publications.
source: To bridge this gap, we use genotypes to derive predicted phenotypes based on a set of rules derived from peer-reviewed publications (see Materials and methods and formal rules definitions available from the article's Resource Page).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for phenotype prediction.

claim: Critical variants for drug resistance prediction include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13, crt, dhfr, dhps, as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in kelch13 are associated with resistance to artemisinin.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mutations in crt are associated with resistance to chloroquine.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug resistance markers.

claim: Mutations in dhfr are associated with resistance to pyrimethamine.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug resistance markers.

claim: Mutations in dhps are associated with resistance to sulfadoxine.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug resistance markers.

claim: An amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 is a marker of resistance to piperaquine.
source: These critical variants include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in genes kelch13 (resistance to artemisinin), (Ariey et al., 2014) crt (chloroquine), dhfr (pyrimethamine), dhps (sulfadoxine), as well as an amplification breakpoint sequence in plasmepsin2/3 (marker of resistance to piperaquine) (Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Artemisinin resistance (ART-R) has reached very high levels in the lower Mekong region (Cambodia, northeastern Thailand, southern Laos, and Vietnam).
source: The resulting map indicates that ART-R has reached very high levels in the lower Mekong region (Cambodia, northeastern Thailand, southern Laos, and Vietnam), nearing fixation in Cambodia and around its borders, with the exception of very few provinces of Laos and the Vietnam coast (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: ART-R is nearing fixation in Cambodia and around its borders.
source: The resulting map indicates that ART-R has reached very high levels in the lower Mekong region (Cambodia, northeastern Thailand, southern Laos, and Vietnam), nearing fixation in Cambodia and around its borders, with the exception of very few provinces of Laos and the Vietnam coast (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: No samples in this study were predicted to be ART-R in India and Bangladesh.
source: Predicted ART-R frequencies decline to the west of this region: no samples in this study were predicted to be ART-R in India and Bangladesh, thus showing no evidence of spread beyond the GMS, or of local emergence of resistant parasite populations.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the absence of ART-R in certain regions.

claim: There is no evidence of ART-R spread beyond the GMS to India and Bangladesh, or of local emergence of resistant parasite populations in these countries.
source: Predicted ART-R frequencies decline to the west of this region: no samples in this study were predicted to be ART-R in India and Bangladesh, thus showing no evidence of spread beyond the GMS, or of local emergence of resistant parasite populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ART-R markers in samples from these countries.

claim: The kelch13 C580Y mutation is the dominant allele in the lower Mekong region.
source: An analysis of the distribution of kelch13 ART-R alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3) reveals a marked difference between the lower Mekong region, where the kelch13 C580Y mutation is the dominant allele, and the region comprising Myanmar and western Thailand, where a wide variety of non-synonymous kelch13 variants are found, and C580Y is not dominant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: In Myanmar and western Thailand, a wide variety of non-synonymous kelch13 variants are found, and C580Y is not dominant.
source: An analysis of the distribution of kelch13 ART-R alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3) reveals a marked difference between the lower Mekong region, where the kelch13 C580Y mutation is the dominant allele, and the region comprising Myanmar and western Thailand, where a wide variety of non-synonymous kelch13 variants are found, and C580Y is not dominant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The recent increase of C580Y mutant prevalence in Cambodia and neighboring regions results from the rapid spread of the KEL1/PLA1 strain of multidrug-resistant parasites.
source: This reflects a recent increase of C580Y mutant prevalence in Cambodia and neighboring regions, resulting from the rapid spread of the KEL1/PLA1 strain of multidrug-resistant parasites (Hamilton et al., 2019; Amato et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The KEL1/PLA1 hard selection sweep has replaced a variety of ART-R alleles previously present in Cambodia and neighboring regions.
source: This hard selection sweep has replaced a variety of ART-R alleles previously present in that region, resulting from multiple soft sweeps (Miotto et al., 2015; Miotto et al., 2013); this process has not occurred along the Thai-Myanmar border, where allele diversity is still very pronounced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The hard selection sweep process has not occurred along the Thai-Myanmar border, where allele diversity is still very pronounced.
source: This hard selection sweep has replaced a variety of ART-R alleles previously present in that region, resulting from multiple soft sweeps (Miotto et al., 2015; Miotto et al., 2013); this process has not occurred along the Thai-Myanmar border, where allele diversity is still very pronounced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research and data from the study.

claim: Parasites carrying both kelch13 C580Y and plasmepsin2/3 amplification are confined to a well-defined area of the lower Mekong region.
source: Mapping the combined presence of C580Y and plasmepsin2/3 amplification shows that parasites carrying both markers are confined to a well-defined area of the lower Mekong region, and these resistant strains have not made their way into provinces of Laos and Vietnam where ART-R and PPQ-R alleles circulate separately (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: DHA-PPQ resistant strains have not made their way into provinces of Laos and Vietnam where ART-R and PPQ-R alleles circulate separately.
source: Mapping the combined presence of C580Y and plasmepsin2/3 amplification shows that parasites carrying both markers are confined to a well-defined area of the lower Mekong region, and these resistant strains have not made their way into provinces of Laos and Vietnam where ART-R and PPQ-R alleles circulate separately (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Decades after the replacement of chloroquine as frontline therapy, the frequency of parasites predicted to be resistant (CQ-R) remains exceptionally high across the GMS.
source: The resulting data show that, decades after the replacement of chloroquine as frontline therapy, the frequency of parasites predicted to be resistant (CQ-R) remains exceptionally high across the GMS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The continued use of chloroquine as frontline treatment for P. vivax malaria could be a major contributing factor to sustained levels of CQ-R in P. falciparum.
source: The reasons for such sustained levels of resistance are unclear; the continued use of chloroquine as frontline treatment for P. vivax malaria, and the low diversity associated with the extremely high prevalence of resistant haplotypes could be major contributing factors.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for sustained CQ-R levels.

claim: Low diversity associated with the extremely high prevalence of resistant haplotypes could be a major contributing factor to sustained levels of CQ-R.
source: The reasons for such sustained levels of resistance are unclear; the continued use of chloroquine as frontline treatment for P. vivax malaria, and the low diversity associated with the extremely high prevalence of resistant haplotypes could be major contributing factors.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for sustained CQ-R levels.

claim: High levels of dhfr and dhps markers associated with resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) were found in the GMS.
source: Similarly, we found high levels of the dhfr and dhps markers associated with resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP, Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Predicted resistance to SP is lowest in India, where SP is still used with artesunate as the frontline ACT.
source: It is interesting that predicted resistance is lowest in India, where SP is still used with artesunate as the frontline ACT (Directorate of National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme DGoHS and Government of India, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation about treatment policy.

claim: In Vietnam, sample collections were carried out by two NMCP institutes (IMPE-QN and NIMPE), covering approximately 70 sites in seven provinces.
source: In Vietnam, sample collections were carried out by two NMCP institutes (IMPE-QN and NIMPE), covering approximately 70 sites in seven provinces.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study implementation in Vietnam.

claim: Prior to GenRe-Mekong surveillance, evidence of artemisinin resistance had been found in the Vietnamese provinces of Binh Phuoc, Gia Lai, Dak Nong, Khanh Hoa, and Ninh Thuan.
source: Prior to this surveillance activity, evidence of artemisinin resistance had been found in the provinces of Binh Phuoc, Gia Lai, Dak Nong, Khanh Hoa, and Ninh Thuan province (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a WHO report.

claim: GenRe-Mekong data showed that the province of Dak Lak also has extremely high levels of predicted ART-R.

source: Given the very recent aggressive spread of DHA-PPQ-R strains, it is likely that ART-R parasites in the Upper Zone are remnants of an earlier sweep which may also have spread from the south, as suggested by the higher frequency in Salavan province than in Savannakhet.
evidence: This is speculation based on the geographical distribution of drug resistance markers.

claim: A genetic barcode tree clearly separates Upper Zone and Lower Zone parasites in Laos.
source: To confirm the presence of distinct ART-R populations, we used genetic barcodes to construct a tree that recapitulates population structure in Laos (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which clearly separates Upper Zone and Lower Zone parasites.

claim: DHA-PPQ-R parasites in Laos form a large, tight cluster clearly separated from the kelch13 wild-type samples from the Upper Zone.

claim: The northward spread of DHA-PPQ-R strains in Laos has likely been contained by the use of artemether-lumefantrine.

evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the geographical distribution of drug resistance.
